summary: A 1975 set of comments on the host and IMP protocol changes proposed in RFC 687. It is updated by RFC 692. See also RFC 696.

plainLanguage.summary: One engineer proposed changes to the rules that connect a computer to its network router. This memo repeats each proposal and adds a short comment on it, agreeing with most of them but warning that the changes would take a lot of programming work.

subtitle: Jon Postel annotates a proposed list of Host/IMP protocol changes, point by point.

tldr.problem: RFC 687 proposed a set of changes to the protocol between hosts and their IMPs, and its author wanted feedback on the plan.
tldr.mechanism: Postel reproduces each point and adds a comment underneath, mostly approving but questioning some field sizes, the packets-per-message control, and the effect on the host-to-host protocol.
tldr.outcome: He calls it a fine set of suggestions, but estimates the work at a lower bound of about 48 person-months of system programmer time.

sections.title: What the Comments Cover
sections.content: This memo is a set of comments by Jon Postel on Dave Walden's RFC 687, which suggests changes to the host-IMP protocol. Walden's points are reproduced with Postel's comments underneath. The numbering jumps from 9 to 11, and the text asks "What happened to 10?".
sections.plainLanguage: The memo copies a proposed list of changes and writes a short response under each item. One numbered item is missing from the list, and the author notices.

sections.title: Leader, Address and Header Fields
sections.content:
The proposal expands the leader from two to five 16-bit words and the address field to 24 bits, made of 16 bits of IMP address and 8 bits of host address. A new optional message length field, 13 bits wide, would let the source host tell the subnetwork the message length in bits. The handling type field grows to eight bits to allow parallel message streams with different handling.

Postel notes that a five-word leader plus the existing 40-bit host header gives a prefix of 120 bits, not the neat 72-bit boundary the current protocol has, unless the host header grows to 64 bits for 144 in total. He concedes the 24-bit address space of 16,777,216 is big, but says an extensible scheme might be more appropriate, and suggests a 16-bit length field.
sections.plainLanguage: The plan makes the address and the message header larger. Postel asks whether the new sizes line up neatly, and whether the length field should be a little wider.

sections.title: Other Changes and Compatibility
sections.content:
Further proposals include letting the source host specify how many packets make up a multi-packet message, making unordered (type-3) messages a handling type rather than a message type, redefining fake host addresses without the For/From IMP bit, adding a parameter to the IMP-to-host NOP, and a non-blocking host interface so the IMP can refuse a message without blocking and ask the host to resend it.

Old and new formats would run in parallel, with the host choosing the mode through its host-to-IMP NOP message. Postel finds this difficult to implement but crucial to have. He questions the packets-per-message control, since the new message length field could serve the same purpose, and approves most of the rest.
sections.plainLanguage: Old and new ways of talking would work side by side for a while, so nobody has to switch over on the same day. Postel thinks this is hard to build but necessary.

sections.title: The Cost of the Changes
sections.content:
Postel's overall view is that this is a fine set of suggestions, but he is concerned about the host-to-host protocol changes that it implies or makes more desirable. His rough guess is a couple of person-months of system programmer time for each operating system on the network.

With 24 systems at 2 person-months each, that is 48 person-months, or 4 person-years, and he says this may be the lower bound.
sections.plainLanguage: Even a good plan means work for every computer on the network. He adds up the months of programming and warns the total could be higher.
